breadcrumb.current: Everything we shipped at Summit this year and how the pieces fit

header.title: Everything we shipped at Summit this year and how the pieces fit

blocks.text: Ten years ago a handful of analysts started writing transformations the way software teams write code: in version control, with tests, reviewed by a colleague before anything reached production. That habit spread into a discipline, and the discipline grew into a community that now spans many thousands of practitioners.

The job has changed again since then. Teams now answer questions for people, for applications and, more and more often, for automated agents that read the same tables at machine speed. Each of those consumers needs the same thing: numbers that are defined once, tested on every change and explained well enough that nobody has to guess what a column means.

This year at Summit more than two thousand people joined us in person and many more followed online. We used the keynote to show how Lattice is growing to meet that moment, from a much faster engine to context that agents can read safely. Below is the full list of what we announced, with links to the [release notes](/blog) and to the sessions where you can see each feature running against a real project.
A faster core engine
Lattice Core 2.0 compiles very large projects in seconds

Most of the time a data team spends waiting is not spent in the warehouse. It is spent parsing, compiling and resolving a project before a single query runs. Lattice Core 2.0 is a ground-up rewrite of that path. On a project with eight thousand models, a full parse that used to take close to two minutes now finishes in under four seconds, and editing a single file updates the graph almost instantly.

The new engine is **available today for every account** on the platform and as an open download for local work. It reads existing projects without changes, and the [upgrade guide](/resources/analytics-lifecycle) covers the handful of deprecated settings.

video.alt: Video: a tour of the new core engine

blocks.text: Read the [full engine release notes](/blog).

items.text: The open core is published under the same permissive licence as before, so community packages, adapters and the command line keep working exactly the way they do today, now with the faster parser underneath them.
The hosted platform adds caching, remote execution and a shared index across environments.

blocks.text: Both editions share one language and one project format, so moving work between a laptop and the platform needs no rewrite at all.
Supported warehouses:

items.text: Cobalt DB, Northwind, Quarry and Helixa are generally available.
Stratus and the Driftway lake format are in beta and open to every account.
Two further engines are planned for spring.

blocks.text: Our nightly project has grown to nearly six thousand models, and compile time had quietly become the slowest part of every change. On the new engine our editor feels instant again, and the full parse finishes before I have switched windows. Nobody on the team asked for a faster tool, but everybody noticed the day we turned it on. — Priya Raman, Head of Analytics Engineering, Kestrel
Try it on [your own project](/signup).
State-aware builds everywhere: rebuild only what has actually changed

Last year we introduced state-aware orchestration for a small group of design partners. It is now **on by default for new projects** and one setting away for existing ones. Before each run Lattice compares sources and code to the last successful build and skips every model whose inputs are unchanged, which is usually most of them. Teams in the beta cut [warehouse spend](/product/cost-optimization) by a **third on average**.

We expected faster runs. What surprised us was the bill. Half our models now skip on a typical night because nothing upstream changed, and the warehouse spend for the team dropped by more than a third in the first month. We spent that budget on two projects that had been waiting in the backlog all year. — Tomas Ekberg, Director of Data Platforms, Meridian Partners

State awareness also changes how freshness works. Instead of scheduling everything on a timer and hoping sources have landed, you can declare how fresh each model needs to be. A model with a `freshness: 1 hour` rule rebuilds when its inputs are newer than that and stays put otherwise. Combined with event-based triggers, nightly jobs become a set of small, cheap runs that happen when data arrives. The run log records every skip with a reason, so it is always clear why a model did or did not build, and the same reasons are available through the API for teams that track cost per model in their own dashboards.

State-aware builds changed the conversation with our finance partners. We no longer defend a number on the monthly invoice; we show them which models ran, why they ran and what each run cost. It is the first time our platform spend has felt like something we control rather than something that just happens to us. — Grace Okafor, Chief Data Officer, Halcyon

video.alt: Video: state-aware builds in a live project

blocks.text: State-aware builds work with every supported warehouse and every scheduler integration. Existing jobs keep their schedules; the skipping happens inside each run with no change to how jobs are configured.
See the [state-aware build documentation](/product/deploy) to switch an existing project over.
Bring your own compute: run each model on the engine that suits the job best

Not every model needs a large warehouse. Many teams run small staging transforms and tests on infrastructure that costs far more than the work requires. Starting this quarter, Lattice can route individual models to a lightweight local engine while heavier joins stay where they are.

You choose per model or per folder with a single setting, `compute: light`, and Lattice moves data between engines through open table formats so nothing is copied by hand. **Lineage, tests and documentation stay in one project**, whichever engine runs a given step. In early trials, teams moved between twenty and forty percent of their models onto lighter compute with no change to results. Routing decisions appear in the run log next to each model, and a dry-run mode shows which models would move before anything changes in production.

Mixed compute is in preview for Cobalt DB and Quarry, with others to follow. Read the [preview announcement](/blog), browse the [supported formats](/data-platforms/cobalt) and sign up for the [office hours](/community) where the engineering team answers questions about early results.
Context that agents can depend on

An assistant can only be as reliable as the context it receives. A project already contains most of what they need: model descriptions, column types, tests, owners and the [metric definitions](/product/semantic-layer) in the semantic layer. *What has been missing is a safe, consistent way to hand that context over.*

The new **context service** exposes a project’s certified models, metrics and lineage through one read-only interface. Agents can ask which table holds weekly revenue, what a column means or whether yesterday’s build passed, and every reply is built on the very definitions your people rely on.

Access follows the permissions you already have. An agent acting for a user sees what that user sees and nothing more, and every request is logged with the question, the objects returned and the identity behind it. We built the service on an open specification so any assistant can connect, including the ones your company builds itself. Lattice Assistant, our own helper inside the editor, now uses the same service, which means its suggestions are drawn from your tests and definitions rather than from guesses about naming conventions. It can draft a model, propose tests for a new column, explain an unfamiliar part of the graph, or summarise why last night’s run failed and which change most likely caused it.

image.alt: An editor with a model, passing tests and an assistant suggestion

blocks.text: The context service is in [public preview](/product/assistant) for every platform account. Assistant features in the editor are generally available, and the [command-line helper](/product/ai) is in beta. To connect a custom agent, start with the `context.read` scope and the [quickstart](/learn). *Pricing for agent requests will be announced before general availability.*
Charts, as code

Dashboards are often the last place where definitions drift. A metric is defined carefully in the project and then rebuilt slightly differently in a reporting tool. Lattice Charts closes that gap by keeping simple visualisations in the same repository as the models that feed them.

A chart is a short YAML file that points at a metric or a model, picks a chart type and sets a few display options. It is versioned, approved alongside the SQL it depends on and built during that same run, so a change to a definition and a change to the chart that shows it ship together. If a test fails, the chart does not update, and readers see a clear note that the last good version is on display.

Charts are not trying to replace every reporting tool. They are meant for the handful of views that matter most and that should never disagree with the project: weekly revenue, active customers, pipeline health. For deeper analysis, the same metrics remain available to any connected tool.

Lattice Charts is in public beta. Any project on the platform can turn it on from the settings page, and a set of starter templates covers line, bar, table and single-number views. We expect general availability early next year, with sharing controls and scheduled exports.
Try [Lattice Charts](/product/charts).

video.alt: Video: building a dashboard from a reviewed model

blocks.text: From model to dashboard in a single review

The common thread in every announcement is the review. A change to a model, its tests, its metric and the chart that shows it should be a single unit of work that a teammate can read, run and approve. When that is true, quality stops depending on heroics.

This year we also made reviews easier to do well. Pull requests now show a rendered diff of affected rows for sampled data, a list of downstream models and charts, and the cost estimate of the change. Reviewers can run a slim build in a private schema with one click and leave comments on specific columns.

We will keep investing here. Next on the list are review checklists that teams can define once, automatic suggestions for missing tests on new columns and a clearer way to roll back a change that slipped through. If you have opinions on any of these, the product team reads every post in the community forum and runs open roadmap sessions each quarter.
Join the [roadmap discussion](/community).
What ships, and when

Everything above is either available now or open for preview. The table lists the current status of each item. Generally available features are covered by standard support; previews and betas are free to try and may change based on feedback before release.
Here is the quickest way to try the new features in your own project:

items.text: [Upgrade to the new engine](/product/develop) from the project settings.
Turn on [state-aware builds](/product/deploy) for one production job and compare the run log against the previous week.
Connect an assistant to the [context service](/product/assistant).
Add a first [chart file](/product/charts) next to a metric your team checks every Monday.
Move a folder of staging models to light compute with `compute: light` and watch the cost column in the run history.
Book a [walkthrough](/contact) with a solutions architect.
Watch the [Summit sessions on demand](/resources/on-demand) for deeper dives into each feature, with live demos and the questions the audience asked during the talks.
